hero.title: Taking FIRST to the capitol.
hero.subtitle: GEarheads doesn't just compete in FIRST — we fight for it. Over three consecutive years, our student advocates have walked the halls of the Wisconsin State Capitol, met with federal legislators in Washington D.C., and pushed the policy changes that unlock robotics access for K–12 students across the state and the country.

impact.label: What we secured
impact.text: The DPI Robotics League Bill passed into law — directing $500,000 in annual state funding toward K–12 robotics programs across Wisconsin. Seven GEarheads students mobilized for this effort, meeting with more than 75 state legislators across three years of advocacy work to make it happen.

whyWeAdvocate.heading: Why we advocate
paragraphs: GEarheads competes because FIRST works. The program teaches students to design under constraints, test against data, collaborate across disciplines, and present ideas to adults with real authority. But FIRST only works if teams can afford to participate — and for many Wisconsin schools, the cost of registration fees, field sets, and practice materials is precisely the barrier that keeps programs from starting or continuing. That is the problem our advocacy is designed to solve.

When we show up at the Capitol, we are not asking for favors. We are presenting evidence. We bring participation data, program outcome research, and a direct account of what FIRST has done for our own students — the ones standing in the room making the case. That combination is hard for a legislator to dismiss: here is the evidence that the program works, and here is a student in your district who can tell you firsthand what it means.

The systemic impact of sustained advocacy compounds in ways that a single visit cannot. By returning to the Capitol for a third consecutive year, with updated outcome data and the same faces who built relationships the year before, we converted meetings into trust and trust into legislation. The DPI Robotics League Bill is the result — $500,000 in annual state funding that will outlast any individual team's competitive season and make FIRST accessible to Wisconsin students who have never heard of GEarheads.

Advocacy is also how we practice the skills FIRST teaches. Preparing a policy brief is a design problem. Making the case to a skeptical legislator is a communication challenge. Tracking a bill through committee is project management. Every tool we develop on the robot — systematic analysis, data-driven argument, iterative refinement — applies directly in the policy arena. We advocate because it is effective, and because the work makes us better engineers.

milestones.label:
WI Capitol
Advocacy Day
milestones.summary: Three consecutive years of student voices in the Wisconsin State Capitol.
milestones.detail: FIRST Advocacy Day in Wisconsin sends student robotics teams directly to the Capitol to make the case for FIRST programs to state legislators — in person, face to face. GEarheads has participated for three consecutive years, making us one of the most consistent student advocacy presences in the Wisconsin FIRST community. Each year, team members prepare written testimony and policy briefs, rehearse their talking points with adult mentors, and then walk the marble corridors to meet with their own district representatives as well as key committee chairs. The conversations are substantive: students explain what FIRST programs cost, what they produce, and what funding gaps currently prevent schools from participating. Over three years, we have spoken with more than 75 legislators, building a durable track record of credibility that single-year advocacy trips cannot establish. The cumulative effect — returning faces, consistent messaging, updated outcome data from each season — is precisely what turns a single meeting into a relationship and a relationship into a vote. Year one, legislators are politely curious. Year two, they remember the team. Year three, they sponsor the bill.
highlights: Three consecutive years at the Wisconsin State Capitol
Spoke directly with 75+ state legislators across the three-year streak
Prepared written testimony and policy briefs before each visit
Met with district representatives and key committee members
Built a multi-year credibility track record with the legislature

milestones.label:
FIRST WI
Student Board
milestones.summary: A formal seat on the FIRST Wisconsin Student Board of Directors.
milestones.detail: In addition to showing up on Advocacy Day, GEarheads earned a formal leadership seat on the FIRST Wisconsin Student Board of Directors — the organized body of student representatives who shape FIRST Wisconsin's strategic direction, advocacy priorities, and community programming. A seat on this board means GEarheads is not just a participant in FIRST Wisconsin: we help decide what FIRST Wisconsin advocates for at the state level, how new programs are structured, and how student voices are represented in conversations with adult administrators and state officials. Board membership requires sustained commitment across a full season, attendance at board meetings, and active participation in planning sessions. For a team from Brookfield, having this institutional seat ensures that our community's perspective — suburban, mid-size district, resource-constrained in ways that differ from large urban or rural districts — is consistently in the room when statewide decisions are made. The board also provides a direct line into FIRST national policy conversations, because FIRST Wisconsin's student leadership connects upward into the broader national FIRST advocacy network. What begins at a board meeting in Madison can shape the framing of federal testimony in Washington.
highlights: Formal seat on the FIRST Wisconsin Student Board of Directors
Shapes FIRST Wisconsin's advocacy agenda and community programs
Ensures Elmbrook district perspective is represented statewide
Sustained multi-meeting commitment across a full season
Bridges the gap between team-level and state-level FIRST leadership

milestones.label:
Governor's Cup
Washington D.C.
milestones.summary: An hour with Governor Evers and his policy staff in Washington D.C.
milestones.detail: The FIRST Governor's Cup Washington D.C. trip takes a select group of student teams to the nation's capital to advocate for STEM funding and robotics policy at the federal level. GEarheads participated and secured a meeting that ran for more than an hour with Governor Tony Evers, his spouse, and two members of his policy staff. This was not a photo opportunity: it was a working policy conversation. Students presented data on participation gaps in Wisconsin robotics, made the case for state-level investment in K–12 FIRST programs, and specifically raised the need for the DPI Robotics League funding expansion that would later become law. The Governor's team engaged directly with the specific proposals, asked follow-up questions, and the meeting extended well past its scheduled time — a signal that the conversation had genuine traction. The Washington trip also included meetings with federal legislators on Capitol Hill, exposing our students to both the federal appropriations process and the interplay between state and federal STEM policy. The experience of articulating a policy proposal to a sitting governor and his staff is transformative: it makes the stakes real in a way no classroom exercise can replicate.
highlights: 1+ hour meeting with Governor Tony Evers and two policy staff members
Presented specific policy proposals on K–12 robotics funding gaps
Meeting extended beyond scheduled time due to depth of discussion
Also met with federal legislators on Capitol Hill
Connected state-level DPI funding effort to federal STEM policy context

milestones.label:
K–12 DPI
Funding Push
milestones.summary: Expanding Wisconsin's robotics funding from grades 6–12 to K–12.
milestones.detail: One of the specific policy changes GEarheads advocated for was the expansion of Wisconsin's Department of Public Instruction robotics funding eligibility from grades 6–12 to cover the full K–12 spectrum — bringing elementary school FIRST LEGO League programs under the same funding umbrella as middle and high school FTC and FRC programs. This matters because the pipeline into competitive robotics depends on early exposure. Students who first encounter FIRST in elementary school through FLL are dramatically more likely to progress through the program levels, stay involved through high school, and carry those skills into post-secondary education and careers. By limiting eligibility to grade 6 and above, the prior policy left the most critical on-ramp unfunded and dependent on individual school or parent fundraising. Our advocacy specifically named this gap, provided data on FIRST Wisconsin FLL participation trends, and made the case that the investment in K–12 coverage would yield compounding returns across the full pipeline — not just at the high school competition level. The expanded eligibility means that a fifth-grade student in a Wisconsin elementary school now has a path to a funded FLL team, which becomes the on-ramp to FTC, which becomes the pipeline to college engineering programs and STEM careers.
highlights: Advocated for expanding DPI eligibility from grades 6–12 to K–12
Named the FLL funding gap as a pipeline problem, not just an access problem
Provided FIRST Wisconsin enrollment data to support the expansion case
Connected elementary-level FLL investment to high school FTC/FRC pipeline outcomes
Addressed the full FIRST program spectrum, not just competitive robotics

milestones.label:
Chips &
Sciences Act
milestones.summary: One of five teams nationally to advocate for the Chips & Sciences Act.
milestones.detail: At the federal level, GEarheads was selected as one of only five robotics teams in the country to participate in advocacy efforts tied to the CHIPS and Science Act — the landmark federal legislation that directed roughly $280 billion toward semiconductor manufacturing, scientific research, and STEM workforce development in the United States. Our specific role was to advocate for the portions of the Act that fund K–12 STEM education pipelines, making the case to federal legislators that FIRST robotics programs are exactly the kind of applied STEM experience the legislation is designed to generate. Six federal legislators were engaged across these meetings. The national scope of this effort put GEarheads in conversation with federal appropriations staff and policy aides about a pool of educational programming funding that flows from the Act. Being one of five teams selected for this advocacy signals the credibility our team has built not just within Wisconsin, but within the national FIRST policy community. The conversations at this level differ from state advocacy: the questions are sharper, the policy landscape is more complex, and the documentation requirements are higher. Our preparation — detailed data, a clear ask, and a practiced delivery — allowed our students to hold their own in rooms that most high school students never enter.
highlights: One of only 5 robotics teams nationally selected for Chips & Sciences Act advocacy
Met with 6 federal legislators on Capitol Hill
Advocated for the K–12 STEM pipeline provisions within the Act
Engaged with federal educational programming funding tied to the legislation
Signals national-level credibility within the FIRST policy community

milestones.label:
DPI Robotics
League Bill
milestones.summary: The bill passed. $500,000 in annual state funding secured.
milestones.detail: The culmination of three years of state-level advocacy work was the passage of the DPI Robotics League Bill — a piece of Wisconsin legislation that directs $500,000 in annual state funding toward K–12 robotics programs administered through the Department of Public Instruction. This is not a grant program or a pilot: it is permanent statutory funding, meaning programs that qualify can plan and budget around it year over year. Seven GEarheads students were directly involved in the advocacy push that contributed to the bill's passage: presenting testimony, meeting with sponsor legislators, tracking committee progress, and maintaining relationships with legislative offices through the multi-session journey from introduction to floor vote. The $500K annual appropriation funds FIRST registration fees, field sets, practice materials, and program coordination — precisely the categories that price smaller or newer teams out of participation. The bill's passage is the clearest proof of what sustained, data-driven, relationship-built student advocacy can achieve: real law, real money, real access for the next generation of Wisconsin robotics teams. Every future FTC team that forms because their school could finally afford the registration has, in some small part, the GEarheads advocacy class to thank.
highlights: $500,000 annual state funding directed to K–12 robotics programs — passed into law
7 GEarheads students directly involved in the legislative push
Permanent statutory funding, not a one-time grant
Covers registration fees, field sets, and program materials that price teams out
Three years of consistent advocacy converted into a signed bill
